title: Set Work Study: Beethoven's Pathétique Sonata, First Movement
content_html:
Beethoven, Vienna and the Public Drama of the Sonata

By 1798, when he composed the Pathétique Sonata, Beethoven had settled in Vienna as a rising pianist-composer, building a reputation for fiery improvisation and technically daring keyboard writing. Published in 1799 with a dedication to his patron Prince Karl von Lichnowsky, the sonata was Beethoven’s own title choice — ‘Grande Sonate Pathétique’ — and it announces a new kind of ambition for the genre. Where earlier Classical sonatas by Haydn and Mozart were often intimate, domestic music, Beethoven treats the piano sonata as a public, theatrical statement, full of the same drama and scale audiences expected from a symphony or opera.

This is instrumental music from the Classical era, written for a solo pianist rather than an orchestra or singer, and it belongs to the broader Instrumental Music 1700–1820 area of study alongside Bach’s Brandenburg Concerto. Where Bach’s concerto relies on the interplay of multiple instrumental lines within a Baroque concerto grosso texture, Beethoven’s sonata explores what a single performer can achieve on one instrument — contrast, weight, silence and sudden shock are all generated by one pair of hands.

Key fact: the work is a piano sonata in three movements, but your set work focuses only on the first movement, which combines a slow Grave introduction with a fast sonata-form Allegro.

The Grave Introduction: Beethoven's Radical Opening

The movement opens with a slow, weighty Grave section in common time, marked by dotted rhythms, thick low chords and sudden dynamic contrasts between forte and piano. This alone was not unusual for the period — French overtures and some symphonies used slow introductions — but what is radical is that Beethoven brings this Grave material back later in the movement, rather than leaving it behind once the fast music begins. This blurs the boundary between introduction and main structure, making the Grave feel like a recurring character in the drama rather than a throat-clearing preamble.

After the Grave, the music launches into the Allegro di molto e con brio, and the contrast could not be more extreme: tempo, dynamic and texture all change abruptly, throwing the listener from brooding stillness into restless energy. This whiplash effect, achieved purely through structural placement and contrast, is one of the most quoted features of the piece in music history because it shows Beethoven treating musical elements themselves as dramatic tools.

As you listen to a full performance of the movement, track the Grave material every time it returns: notice how its slow tempo and dense chords act almost like a scene change in a play, briefly halting the forward drive of the Allegro before the fast tempo resumes with renewed intensity. Listen out especially for the tremolo bass figures and sudden pianissimo-to-fortissimo shifts in the fast sections, since these are exactly the kind of detail examiners expect you to identify by ear.

Key fact: the Grave introduction returns twice more within the movement — once at the very start of the development, and once, very briefly, just before the final coda — giving a sonata-form movement an almost rondo-like sense of recurring framing.

Sonata Form in the Exposition: Two Contrasting Worlds

Once the Allegro begins, the movement follows sonata form, built from an exposition, development and recapitulation. The exposition presents the first subject in the tonic key of C minor: a restless, rising arpeggio-based idea driven forward by an insistent tremolo left hand, giving the texture an almost orchestral tremor beneath the melodic line. This first subject is urgent and unstable, constantly climbing and falling away, embodying the ‘pathetic’ (suffering, passionate) character suggested by the title.

A transition passage then modulates the music towards the second subject group. Rather than settling in the expected relative major of E flat, Beethoven initially places the second subject in E flat minor — a much darker, more unsettled choice that delays the arrival of real major-key relief. Only partway through the second subject does the music brighten into E flat major, and a closing theme in E flat major rounds off the exposition. This slow, hard-won journey towards major-key warmth is a key expressive strategy: brightness has to be earned rather than given freely.

For your listening exam, be ready to identify these two contrasting ideas by ear: the driving, minor-key first subject with its tremolo accompaniment, and the more lyrical, initially minor-mode second subject that eventually turns to major. Comparing their character — urgent versus songful, minor versus shifting to major — is exactly the kind of contrast question that appears in short-answer listening tasks.

Development, Recapitulation and Coda: Drama Resolved

The development section works the first-subject material and fragments of the Grave through a series of modulations, building tension through sequence, imitation between the hands and increasingly unstable harmony. Rather than introducing brand new melodic material, Beethoven intensifies what we already know, a typical Classical development technique, but pushed here towards greater drama and dynamic extremes.

The recapitulation restates the first subject in C minor as expected, but Beethoven reworks the tonal plan of the second subject group: instead of returning straightforwardly in the tonic, it appears first in F minor before eventually settling into C, so that the final resolution to the tonic feels hard-won rather than automatic. This kind of tonal surprise within an otherwise conventional recapitulation shows Beethoven treating sonata form as a flexible dramatic shape rather than a rigid template.

A short coda, built from first-subject material and marked with the same fiery tempo as the main Allegro, brings the movement to its close in C minor, the darker home key winning out over any earlier brightness. The very last, fleeting appearance of the Grave material just before this coda offers one final moment of held-breath stillness before the movement’s energetic, unresolved-sounding conclusion.

The Piano Writing: Technique as Expression

Beethoven exploits the full range and power of the late-eighteenth-century piano to create drama. Tremolo figures in the left hand, rapid repeated notes or octaves, generate a shuddering, orchestral intensity beneath the melodic lines, almost imitating tremolo strings in an orchestra. Sudden dynamic contrasts — fortissimo chords crashing against sections marked piano or pianissimo — create the shock and unpredictability that became a Beethoven trademark, moving well beyond the more even, terraced dynamics typical of earlier Classical style.

Full, widely spaced chords spanning much of the keyboard give the texture real weight and power, while chromatic harmony — notes outside the home key woven into melodic and harmonic lines — adds intense colour and instability, especially in the Grave and development sections. Sforzando accents placed on unexpected beats disrupt the sense of regular metre, adding to the sense of struggle and unpredictability that defines the whole movement.

Key fact: tremolo, subito dynamic contrasts, wide-spanning chords and chromatic harmony are the four piano-writing features examiners most frequently expect you to name when describing the texture and expressive effect of this set work.

Bringing It Together for Your Listening Exam

When answering questions on this set work, always link the musical feature you have heard to its dramatic effect: do not just say ‘tremolo’, explain that the tremolo bass creates tension and forward drive beneath the first subject. Similarly, do not just say ‘sonata form’; be ready to name which section you are hearing — exposition, development or recapitulation — and describe what happens to the first and second subjects within it.

Revise the recurring Grave material as a structural landmark: if you can recognise its distinctive slow tempo, dotted rhythms and dense chords whenever it reappears, you will be able to orientate yourself within the movement’s overall shape even under exam pressure, and this structural awareness often unlocks higher-mark extended answers.
exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to compare the exposition and recapitulation, do not simply restate 'it happens again' — name the specific tonal change (the second subject shifting from E flat minor/major in the exposition to F minor before resolving to C in the recapitulation) since examiners reward precise, named harmonic detail far more highly than vague recognition that 'the theme comes back'.
conclusion_html: You now have the context, structure and pianistic detail needed to discuss this set work confidently; next, practise listening to short extracts and identifying whether you are in the Grave, exposition, development, recapitulation or coda before moving on to compare it with the other Instrumental Music set work.

practice_questions.text: Name the key in which the first subject of the exposition is heard.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying C minor.

practice_questions.text: Describe the tonal journey of the second subject group within the exposition.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for identifying the initial key (E flat minor) and 1 mark for noting the shift to E flat major.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Beethoven creates a dramatic effect at the start of the Allegro section.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for identifying the contrast in tempo and dynamics with the Grave, plus explanation of the shock/drama this creates for the listener.

practice_questions.text: Identify two piano-writing techniques Beethoven uses to build tension in this movement.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark each for any two of: tremolo, subito dynamic contrast, wide chordal spacing, chromatic harmony, sforzando accents.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the recurring Grave material is significant to the structure of the movement.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for identifying where it returns (at the start of the development, and before the coda), and for explaining its framing/dramatic effect on the overall sonata-form structure.

practice_questions.text: Compare the character of the first and second subjects in the exposition.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for contrasting features such as tempo feel, mode, accompaniment texture and emotional character, with reference to specific musical detail.

knowledge_checks.q: In which key is the first movement of the Pathétique Sonata written?
What unusual structural feature does Beethoven include regarding the slow introduction?
options: It is played by an orchestra
It returns later in the movement
It is omitted from the recapitulation
It is played twice as fast each time

knowledge_checks.q: What key does the second subject initially appear in during the exposition?
Which piano technique creates a shuddering, orchestral effect beneath the first subject?
What is the overall form of the first movement?

glossary_terms.definition: A very slow, solemn tempo marking, used here for the movement's dramatic introduction.
A structure of exposition, development and recapitulation used to organise contrasting musical ideas.
The opening section of sonata form where the first and second subjects are presented.
The section of sonata form where earlier musical ideas are fragmented, modulated and intensified.
The section of sonata form where the exposition's material returns, usually in the tonic key.
A concluding passage that rounds off a movement, often reinforcing the home key.
A rapid repetition of a note, octave or chord used to create tension or intensity.
Harmony that uses notes outside the prevailing key to add colour, tension or instability.
An instruction meaning 'suddenly', often applied to abrupt dynamic changes.
A sudden, strong accent placed on a note or chord.
The home key of a piece of music, to which the harmony ultimately returns.
A major and minor key that share the same key signature, such as C minor and E flat major.

description: This lesson unpacks the context, sonata-form structure and dramatic piano writing of the first movement of Beethoven's Piano Sonata No. 8 in C minor 'Pathétique' for your listening exam.

In which city and year was the Pathétique Sonata composed and published?

flashcard_questions.a: It appears first in F minor before resolving to C.
flashcard_questions.q: What happens to the key of the second subject group when it returns in the recapitulation?
